::: {.lead}
Today there are no new ideas. You use what Lecture 11 taught (the logical
operators, brackets, IF–THEN rules and truth tables) on the rules of games:
you write them as conditions, go from a truth table back to a condition,
test a door with every row of its table, and find which game states break a
rule. Do each activity alone. The results of the activities are at the end
of this worksheet: try first, then compare.
:::

## Recall

- NOT `!p`, AND `p && q`, OR `p || q`, XOR `p ^ q`.
- p → q is false only when p is true and q is false.
- The order is NOT, AND, OR; brackets first.
- A truth table with n variables has 2^n rows; its true rows show when a
  rule fires.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Recall"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="6|p || q"}
How many rows has the table of 3 variables?
:   8

    Why: 2 × 2 × 2.

Which C# condition means "exactly one of p and q"?
:   p ^ q

    Why: XOR is true when exactly one is true.

p = T, q = F. What is p → q?
:   false

    Why: that is the only case that breaks an IF–THEN rule.
:::
:::

## Activity 1 · Rules in game code

A farm game has these game states as `bool` variables: `isDay`, `inFight`,
`hasSeeds`, `hasWater`, `isRaining`. The designer writes the rules in words.

![The value of NOT, AND and OR in each case.](images/not-and-or.png){width=80%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 1 · Words to code · 10 min"}
Write each rule as a C# condition.

1. The shop is open when it is day and the player is not in a fight.
2. The player can plant when there are seeds and (water or rain).
3. The scarecrow warning shows when it is night or the player is in a fight.
4. A crop grows when it is raining or the player has water, but not both
   (too much water drowns it).

*Your product:* four conditions.

::: {.check}
1. `isDay && !inFight`. 2. `hasSeeds && (hasWater || isRaining)`: the
brackets are needed. 3. `!isDay || inFight`. 4. `isRaining ^ hasWater`:
"but not both" is XOR.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Code"}
Choose the right condition.

::: {.match extra="hasSeeds && hasWater || isRaining|isDay || !inFight"}
"Plant when there are seeds and water or rain."
:   hasSeeds && (hasWater || isRaining)

    Why: without brackets, rain alone would allow planting with no seeds.

"Open when it is day and the player is not in a fight."
:   isDay && !inFight

    Why: "and" is &&, "not" is !.

"Exactly one of two switches is up."
:   left ^ right

    Why: "exactly one" is XOR.
:::
:::

## Activity 2 · From a truth table back to a condition

Sometimes the designer gives a table: "open in these cases". The programmer
writes one AND for each **true row**, with ¬ in front of each variable that
is F in that row, and joins the ANDs with OR.

![Two true rows give (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ (¬p ∧ q).](images/table-to-rule.png){width=80%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 2 · Table to condition · 12 min"}
1. A lock opens only in the rows (T, F) and (F, T) of p, q. Write the
   condition with one AND per row. Which single operator is it?
2. A door opens only in the rows (T, T) and (F, F) of p, q. Write the
   condition. What does the door check in words?
3. Check one of them in **Truth Table Lab**.

*Your product:* two conditions, one operator and one sentence.

::: {.check}
1. (p ∧ ¬q) ∨ (¬p ∧ q): this is p XOR q. 2. (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q): the door
opens when p and q have the same value (both true or both false).
:::
:::

{{< sim file="sims/truth-table-lab.html" poster="sims/truth-table-lab.png" title="Truth Table Lab: every case of a condition" height="700" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · Back to a condition"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="p ∧ q|p ∨ q"}
The true row (T, F). Its AND?
:   p ∧ ¬q

    Why: ¬ in front of the variable that is F.

True rows (T, F) and (F, T). One operator?
:   p XOR q

    Why: exactly one of p and q is true.

The only true row is (F, F). The condition?
:   ¬p ∧ ¬q

    Why: both variables are F in that row.
:::
:::

## Activity 3 · Every row is a test case

A tester uses the truth table as a test plan: each row is a situation with
the result that the table predicts. The dock door rule is p ∧ (q ∨ r) (pass,
shields up, officer on board), but the code says
`if (hasPass && shieldsUp || officer)`.

![Test cases from the table of the dock door.](images/test-cases.png){width=80%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 3 · Find the bug · 12 min"}
1. Test the row (F, F, T): no pass, no shields, an officer. What does the
   table say? What does the code do?
2. Write the corrected condition.
3. Write four test cases for the repair bay (d ∧ ¬e) ∨ o: two true rows and
   two false rows, each with its expected result.

*Your product:* one bug with its fix, and four test cases.

::: {.check}
Row (F, F, T): the table says **shut**, but the code opens the door: && is
computed first, so `… || officer` is true. Fix:
`hasPass && (shieldsUp || officer)`. Repair bay, for example: (T, F, F) open;
(F, F, T) open; (T, T, F) shut; (F, T, F) shut.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Testing"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="only the true rows|8"}
Why test the false rows too?
:   to see that it does not fire when it should not

    Why: a rule can be wrong by firing in a false row.

How many test cases cover every case of a 3-condition rule?
:   8

    Why: one for each row: 2^3.

The code `hasPass && shieldsUp || officer` opens for an officer alone. Why?
:   && is computed before ||

    Why: it means (hasPass && shieldsUp) || officer.
:::
:::

## Activity 4 · IF–THEN rules in a quest

A quest has two rules: "If the player has the map, then the cave is shown"
and "If the dragon is awake, then the music is loud". A tester writes down
four game states.

![XOR and IF–THEN.](images/xor-implies.png){width=78%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 4 · Which states break a rule? · 10 min"}
Game states (map, cave shown, dragon awake, music loud):
A (T, T, F, F); B (T, F, T, T); C (F, T, T, F); D (F, F, F, F).

1. For each state, is rule 1 kept? Is rule 2 kept?
2. Write the C# condition that finds a broken rule 1.

*Your product:* a table of four states with "kept" or "broken", and one
condition.

::: {.check}
A: both kept (the dragon is asleep, so rule 2 says nothing). B: rule 1
broken (map, but no cave). C: rule 2 broken (dragon awake, music not loud).
D: both kept. Condition: `hasMap && !caveShown`.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Rules kept or broken"}
Choose the right answer. You can use an answer more than once.

::: {.match extra="both broken"}
State B (map, no cave). Rule 1?
:   broken

    Why: T → F is false.

State D (no map, no cave). Rule 1?
:   kept

    Why: F → F is true: the rule says nothing without the map.

State C (dragon awake, music not loud). Rule 2?
:   broken

    Why: T → F is false.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note .ai-task title="Task with AI · A test plan for a big rule"}
**Goal:** the full truth table and test plan of a rule with four conditions:
16 rows by hand is long; an AI assistant writes them, and you check them.

1. **Do it yourself:** write a game rule with four conditions in words, for
   example "the boss door opens when the player has the key and (the boss
   is awake or the timer is 0), and the player is not invisible".
2. **Ask the AI:** start with this prompt and add your rule.

   ::: {.prompt}
   Write the rule below as a condition with the variables p, q, r, s, then
   make its full truth table with 16 rows in the usual order (the first
   column half T, half F). Mark the rows where the rule is true. Then list
   the test cases a tester should run. Rule:
   :::

3. **Check:** check three rows by hand, one of them a true row. Count the
   rows: are there exactly 16, with no row twice? Type the condition into
   **Truth Table Lab** and compare the true rows.

*Your product:* the condition, the table, your three hand checks and one
sentence on any mistake you found.

::: {.check}
A good plan has 16 different rows, the same true rows as Truth Table Lab,
and test cases for the true rows and for the false rows next to them. For
the example rule key ∧ (awake ∨ timer0) ∧ ¬invisible, the door opens in 3 of
16 rows. AI tools often forget the brackets (then extra rows are true) or
repeat a row: look for both.
:::
:::

## Case study: Door Logic

*Torch Hall* is a made-up dungeon game. Its designer writes every door rule
in words: the iron door needs the key and a torch; the wooden door the key
or a torch; a trap fires without a torch; a lever works when exactly one
switch is up; the crown rule says "if crown, then boss defeated"; and the
last gate needs the defeated boss and the key or a torch. The Game challenge
of the interactive page tests these doors with their truth tables.

{{< sim file="sims/door-logic.html" poster="sims/door-logic.png" title="Door Logic: the condition for each door" kind="game" height="640" >}}

## Exercises

1. Write in C#: "the bridge is down when the lever is up or the guard is
   asleep, and the river is not frozen".
2. A rule is true only in the rows (T, T, F) and (F, T, F) of p, q, r. Write
   its condition with one AND per row.
3. The code is `if (hasKey || hasTorch && bossDead)`. Test the row key = T,
   torch = F, boss = F. Is the result right for "boss defeated and key or
   torch"?
4. How many test cases cover every case of a rule with 4 conditions?
5. Rule: "If the shield is up, then the damage is 0." Which state breaks it?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. `(leverUp || guardAsleep) && !riverFrozen`.
2. (p ∧ q ∧ ¬r) ∨ (¬p ∧ q ∧ ¬r) (it is the same as q ∧ ¬r).
3. && first: T || (F && F) = T, but the rule says F (the boss is alive): a bug. Fix: `bossDead && (hasKey || hasTorch)`.
4. 2^4 = 16.
5. The shield is up and the damage is not 0.
:::
